speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Restrictions on air travel have considerably diminished global air cargo capacity and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This has impacted the availability, cost, and timeliness of a connected air freight network.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ports and vessels are not able to continue with usual operational and cost efficiencies as the worsening outbreak hampers logistics chains within countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In Singapore, we have adopted a multi-pronged strategy to deal with this unprecedented disruption to global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The size of our stockpile is determined by a range of factors such as our consumption rate, the supply chain reliability, resupply rate and frequency, shelf life of the products and the cost of storage, the duration of possible disruptions and our local production surge capacities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Maintaining the necessary stockpile for each and every item is a dynamic task that requires constant watch over the fluid global supply situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond the factors mentioned, we must also watch the rising protectionist measures by countries to secure their own supplies which compound the global supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Panic buying will also further distort our usual consumption rate and planning assumptions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the lockdowns in exporting countries persist, the ability of countries to produce and export will come under increasing strain.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For instance, while the Government has worked with Malaysia to ensure that goods, especially food and essentials, continue to flow between our countries following the implementation of Malaysia's Movement Control Order, we cannot be certain how long this will last as the global COVID-19 outbreak continues to escalate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we must certainly plan and be ready for further disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Miss Cheng asked about the key lessons from this episode.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are several learning points for all of us, be it in the Government, business or at the individual level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, panic buying severely disrupts the usual consumption rate and our stockpile efforts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: No amount of stockpile will ever be sufficient if individuals hoard.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, in order for us to not succumb to such fears, we must remind ourselves and each other that collective defence is our strongest defence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can take comfort in the fact that we are not in this battle alone which will help us guard against individual fears and irrational behaviour.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another way to overcome our individual fears is for us to remember the more vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To remember that we all have a responsibility to care for one another, especially in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, we can all play our part by purchasing responsibly and help calm those who are fearful.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, our domestic last mile logistics from the warehouses to the retailers can be disrupted by panic buying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have a finite number of delivery slots, vehicles and drivers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the event of a run on supplies, a vicious cycle is created.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to mobilise logistic players from other sources to help restock our supplies, in turn impacting those supply chains and creating a cascading effect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The compounding disruptions further increase fear and heighten the possibilities of more irrational behaviours.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we are not careful, it becomes a self-fulfilling and self-feeding frenzy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, we can adapt and adjust our consumption choices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, we can switch to frozen or canned options when fresh ones are not available.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can also switch to alternative brands if our preferred ones are not available.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we are adaptable, it strengthens our bargaining position and avoids us being held ransom to price escalation by a few.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fourth, diversification entails our discipline to open up multiple sources of supplies in peacetime, even if it results in slightly higher prices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Otherwise, in a crisis, we will find that we lack alternative supply lines to keep us going.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will then be at the mercy of profiteers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Meanwhile, Singapore is working hard with like-minded partners to ensure that trade continues to flow unimpeded and that critical infrastructure such as the air and seaports remain open to support supply chains globally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This initiative has since gained momentum, with Lao People's Democratic Republic and Uruguay having since come on board.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, we have also kept our trading lines with other countries, such as China and South Korea open.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At last week's G20 Trade Ministers Meeting held via video-conference, the participating Ministers agreed that the world must work together to maintain global productions systems and trade links, there by engendering long-term confidence in investors, businesses and consumers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The outbreak will weigh significantly on global growth, with several major economies expected to go into recession this year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Throughout this crisis, the Government, along with our economic agencies, essential firms, suppliers and logistics providers – both in Singapore and around the world – have been working tirelessly to ensure Singapore continues to function and our shelves remain stocked.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They have shown tremendous ingenuity and tenacity during these unprecedented circumstances, helping secure supplies for us from wherever possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The best way to show our appreciation to them is to treasure what we have been able to obtain despite the circumstances, and never waste any food and materials that they have been able to secure for us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All of us must do our part to support their efforts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Do not panic as our markets, supermarkets and food establishments will continue to operate in spite of the additional precautionary measures from tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must also be psychologically prepared that all of us will need to make adjustments in a crisis.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is another stockpile that people are concerned about which is actually about the mask.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many people read articles that suggested that other countries could be trying to hijack certain goods and products such as N95 masks from Singapore to their countries.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We know that there is a stockpile, but COVID-19 can be here for a long time and what are we doing to protect our healthcare, Police and SCDF personnel?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is a report of mask production lines that were brought back to Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For chronic illness patients as well, such as cancer patients, some face difficulties buying masks or they worry about the quality and source.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, can they get a prescription and buy from public hospitals' pharmacies?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And lastly, what impact with the circuit breaker have on our Singapore economy?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To Miss Cheng's first question about some countries trying to hijack the production of masks, our position to everyone, every country is this: it makes more sense for all of us to work together to keep the supply chains open.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It benefits not just us, it benefits everybody.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But when every country starts to shut down their own production system only for themselves, actually it reduces the entire global capacity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, if I may give an example, one particular country thought that they would keep the intermediate products to themselves and to increase their production capacity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But unfortunately, for that particular country, they do not have the processes for the other intermediate products and in the end they will not able to increase the capacities for everyone or even for themselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is a good lesson for all of us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In order for us to have sufficient for everyone across the entire world, it is essential for every one of us to make sure that we uphold the integrity of the global supply chains, because today, very few of us produce everything ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many of us produce parts of it; the intermediate products, before they go onto the final product.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is how we have approached the issue and this is why we have worked with like-minded partners to make the Joint Ministerial Statement to uphold the integrity of the global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Miss Cheng asked another question about our domestic mask production capacity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would just like to say that, yes, we are building up our own capacity but at this point in time, it will not be appropriate for us to talk about this capacity at this point in time, because we are working with partners to secure the materials, the lines.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But suffice to say that this is something that we have been looking at for some time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Miss Cheng also had a question about vulnerable patients, vulnerable patients who need medical supplies including surgical masks will be able to obtain them from the medical professionals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Miss Cheng's other supplementary question on the cost of goods – how do we keep it stable?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have mentioned, the best ways for us to keep our goods stable are as follows.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, continue to diversify our sources to make sure that we are not held ransom by any one particular source, and this is something that we must do conscientiously even during peacetime, even though it may cause us a bit more during peacetime, because we need to open up multiple channels, as many channels as possible to get our products.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Two, we must make sure that we have some domestic production capability to tide us through difficult moments when we are looking for alternative suppliers; and that applies to keeping the necessary stockpile to buy us time to open up new sources of supply as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Three, we must make sure that we do not panic and give reason for others to hold us ransom because we are unable to share what we have domestically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The final supplementary question from Miss Cheng is on the impact of the circuit breaker measures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will have a very serious impact on our economy but at this point in time, we must understand why we need to do this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we all remain united, if we all take the measures seriously, and if we are successful in controlling the spread in the next one month, then we will be able to progressively resume normalcy and to reduce the impact of the measures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, if we do not take the measures seriously and if in the next one month, we are unable to control the situation, then that might require us to extend the period which such measures are necessary and that will inflict even greater than damage to our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it is in our collective interest to try our best to work together, bear with the inconveniences in the coming month, but let us get over this part together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we can do that, then we can limit further damage to the economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Otherwise, it becomes recurring waves of infections that we have to deal with and it will be very difficult for us to gradually, progressively attain normalcy.
